payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image show visual evidence of a chalk-like drawing treatment applied to the input image?
node.criteria: Pass if the image visibly has a chalk-like drawing appearance; fail if there is sufficient evidence that it remains without a chalk-like drawing treatment; unknown if the image evidence is insufficient to determine this.
node.binding: Compare the edited image with the input image for a chalk-like drawing appearance. Judge the visible result, not a particular technique; unrelated edits do not count as progress.

node_traces.evidence: Compared with the source photo, the edited image has a visibly stylized, chalk-like drawing treatment, with softened sketchy outlines and a grainy, dusty texture across the scene.
Compared with the source photo, the edited image has a visibly stylized, soft, grainy drawing appearance with chalk-like shading and outlines across the giraffes and background.
Compared with the source photo, the edited image has a visibly drawn, chalk-like appearance, with softened grainy shading and sketch-like outlines across the giraffes and background.
Compared with the source photo, the edited image has a visibly softened, grainy, chalk-like drawing treatment across the giraffes and background.
Compared with the photographic source, the edited image has a visibly softened, grainy, hand-drawn appearance with chalk-like shading and outlines across the giraffes and background.

fulfillment: The node’s current criterion treats any chalk-like, whole-image appearance as complete, and the repeated traces show that this wording consistently collapses the result to “yes.” Yet the edited image, while clearly transformed across the scene, retains photographic detail and has a soft, blurred/painterly treatment rather than unambiguously reading as a drawing made from chalk. Refine the typed criterion to distinguish visible progress toward the requested medium from convincing fulfillment of that medium; assess the image’s overall drawing character, not merely grain, softened outlines, or coverage. Preserve partial when evidence supports a real but incomplete transformation, and reserve unknown for genuinely insufficient evidence. Do not infer absence from uncertainty or force a label from the reference alone. The traces are valid and complete, so this is a semantic threshold/evidence-calibration issue, not a transport or dependency failure.
s2: The binding currently emphasizes whether the effect covers the whole image, so repeated traces equate scene-wide grain and softened outlines with complete chalk-drawing fulfillment. Refine the criterion to judge the overall medium transformation against the source: coverage is relevant, but not sufficient; distinguish a genuine yet incomplete stylization from an image that convincingly reads as a chalk-made drawing, considering whether photographic detail and appearance still dominate. Keep partial available when there is clear progress without full fulfillment, and use unknown only when evidence is genuinely insufficient. Do not infer the label from the reference alone or treat low confidence as proof of absence. The traces are valid and complete, so address semantic threshold and evidence calibration, not transport or dependency handling.
